title: How Much Can a Message Carry?
deckline: Group memory created a network. Now the bottleneck was the channel: range, speed, persistence, addressability, and how much meaning one transmission could carry.
objective: Compare nonhuman communication as a family of physical channels with different performance characteristics, using modern species as comparative evidence rather than a chronology, and show the progression from category to location to identity to limited recombination before the undated human-language transition.
learning_outcomes: Keep chronology and comparison separate: these living species are snapshots of communication capabilities, not rungs in historical order.
See communication channels as physical systems with different latency, range, persistence, bandwidth, and detectability.
Recognize that animal messages can carry categories, remote locations, individual identity, and structured combinations without treating those systems as miniature human language.
Identify the next state change: open-ended recombination and shared interpretation vastly expand message capacity in the human lineage.
continuity: Episode 2 showed learned information persisting across seasons and generations as distributed group memory. Episode 3 holds the historical clock mostly still and compares the performance of living communication channels to ask what that distributed network can actually transmit.
future_pressure: The network can warn, point, address, and combine signals, but known nonhuman systems remain far less open-ended than human language. The next episode enters the human lineage without inventing a birthday for language.

slides.title: The network has many incompatible ports

image.alt: A twilight forest meets clear water as a moth, spider, bird, fish, and several mammals exchange subtle light, vibration, posture, and sound patterns through different parts of the scene.

paragraphs: Episode 2 gave us distributed memory. Now stop the historical clock for a moment. The animals in this episode are living examples, not a sequence marching toward humans.

Life communicates through chemistry, color, touch, vibration, electric fields, posture, sound, movement, and combinations of them. Each channel is a different physical port with its own range and limitations.
A message can be a molecule that lingers, a flash that disappears instantly, a vibration that travels through a web, or a call that crosses a dark forest.
The question is no longer whether information can cross between bodies. It is what each channel can carry, how fast, how far, and for how long.

sources.label: Current Biology — Animal signals
sources.note: Reviews animal signaling across chemical, electric, acoustic, optical, and tactile channels.

sources.label: Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology — Ten unanswered questions in multimodal communication
sources.note: Reviews how animals combine and interpret signals across multiple sensory channels.

slides.title: Physics edits every message

image.alt: A forest stream scene shows a scent-like current in the air, a bird call crossing foliage, vibrations passing through a fallen trunk, and broad sound waves moving underwater from a fish.

paragraphs: A chemical mark may persist after the sender leaves, but wind and water smear it. Vision can carry intricate patterns with almost no storage, but only in line of sight. Touch is high-fidelity and nearly zero-range. Vibrations can be excellent if sender and receiver share the right surface.
Sound trades persistence for speed and reach. It vanishes quickly, yet can cross darkness and obstacles. Forests scatter it, wind masks it, and water changes its propagation again.
In computer terms, nature offers no perfect bus. Every channel has latency, range, bandwidth, power cost, and error modes.
Communication systems therefore branch around environments. A whale ocean, bee hive, and monkey forest are different network problems.

sources.label: Journal of Experimental Biology — Acoustic communication in terrestrial and aquatic vertebrates
sources.note: Reviews how the physics of air and water shapes the production, propagation, and detection of animal sounds.

sources.label: Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution — A systems approach to animal communication
sources.note: Treats signaling as a system involving senders, receivers, environments, and multiple interacting channels.

slides.title: A message can carry a category

image.alt: An alert vervet monkey calls while members of the troop look skyward, downward, and toward a tree as an eagle, snake, and leopard appear in different parts of the landscape.

paragraphs: Classic field experiments with vervet monkeys showed that different alarm calls could trigger responses fitted to different predator classes: look up, look down, or move toward trees.

That made the calls famous as functionally referential signals. Later work added useful caution: call use overlaps across contexts, and receivers combine the sound with recent events, social knowledge, and the surrounding scene.
The important upgrade is not a monkey dictionary. The payload can narrow the world into a meaningful category: danger from above rather than below.
A few seconds of sound can save the receiver from having to rediscover the situation from scratch.

sources.label: Science — Monkey responses to three different alarm calls
sources.note: The landmark playback study showing predator-appropriate responses to distinct vervet monkey alarm calls.

sources.label: Scientific Reports — Vervets revisited
sources.note: A quantitative reanalysis showing both predator specificity and important overlap with aggressive contexts.

sources.label: Royal Society Open Science — Context-dependent alarm responses in wild vervet monkeys
sources.note: Tests how listeners combine alarm calls with contextual information.

slides.title: A message can point somewhere else

image.alt: Inside a dark honeybee hive, one forager performs a waggle dance while a luminous geometric echo connects her body angle and movement to a distant flower patch under the sun outside.

paragraphs: Inside a dark honeybee hive, a returning forager can dance about a place that is not there.

The angle of the waggle run carries directional information relative to the sun, while duration varies with distance. Radar-tracking experiments showed recruited bees initially flying the indicated vector before using local cues to finish the search.
This is an addressing upgrade. The sender is not merely saying act now. The message helps the receiver navigate toward a remote target outside the current scene.
The packet is compact and specialized, but it reaches beyond the sender's body and the receiver's immediate view.

sources.label: Nature — The flight paths of honeybees recruited by the waggle dance
sources.note: Radar tracking showed recruited bees flying the vector indicated by a dance before searching near the target.

sources.label: PeerJ — Honey bees communicate distance via non-linear waggle duration functions
sources.note: Explains how body orientation and waggle duration encode direction and distance, including uncertainty in the exact distance function.

slides.title: A message can address one individual

image.alt: Two bottlenose dolphins separated in blue water exchange a distinctive curling whistle pattern that remains recognizable as it crosses the distance between them.

paragraphs: Bottlenose dolphins develop learned, individually distinctive signature whistles. Playback studies show that receivers recognize identity from the whistle's frequency pattern, not only from voice quality.
Dolphins also copy familiar companions' signature whistles, and field experiments support the idea that those copies can be used to address a particular individual.
Calling them names can overstate the evidence, but the information-system point is already strong: a sound pattern can select one social partner from many.
Category, location, identity. The channel is carrying increasingly specific addresses.

sources.label: Proceedings B — Signature whistle shape conveys identity information
sources.note: Playback experiments show dolphins extract identity from signature-whistle shape independently of voice features.

sources.label: PNAS — Bottlenose dolphins can use learned vocal labels to address each other
sources.note: Wild dolphins responded selectively to copies of their own signature whistles.

slides.title: A small repertoire can be recombined

image.alt: A Campbell's monkey calls from a dense rainforest canopy while a few distinct colored sound motifs repeat and join into longer patterned sequences around the troop.

paragraphs: Male Campbell's monkeys produce a small repertoire of alarm and social calls. Researchers found regular modifications and call sequences associated with different contexts.
That matters because the system does not require a completely new signal for every circumstance. A limited inventory can be reused in larger patterns.

Human ears immediately want to install a grammar package. Resist. Researchers disagree about how terms such as syntax and compositionality should be applied across species, and the monkey repertoire remains small and context-bound.
Still, recombination changes the arithmetic. Reuse is a kind of compression: more possible messages from fewer basic units.

sources.label: PLOS ONE — Campbell's monkeys use affixation to alter call meaning
sources.note: Reports predictable changes in call context after an acoustically stable ending is added.

sources.label: PNAS — Campbell's monkeys concatenate vocalizations into context-specific call sequences
sources.note: Describes regular combinations of six call types into context-associated sequences.

sources.label: Biological Reviews — Animal linguistics: a primer
sources.note: Reviews criteria and common pitfalls when applying terms such as semantics, pragmatics, and syntax to animal communication.

slides.title: Then the clock becomes foggy again

image.alt: Across a vast dusk landscape, many animal signal patterns form an unfinished constellation above a small distant group of early humans, suggesting continuity without a staircase or dividing line.

paragraphs: We have now seen messages carry danger, direction, identity, and limited combinations. None of these living species is an earlier chapter of humanity. They show ingredients scattered across animal evolution.

Human language has a radically more open-ended expressive range, but language itself left no fossil. Anatomy, archaeology, genetics, living languages, and comparisons with other animals constrain the story without supplying a date for the first sentence.

So the historical clock becomes uncertain just as message capacity is about to jump. We are moving from deep animal history into millions of years of human-lineage evolution, but not toward a defensible birthday.
The next episode is about the performance change, not an invented timestamp.
